title: Simulating the Evolution of Aggression
beats: Reuses the food/survive/reproduce rules from earlier videos; only change is food comes in pairs
One strategy only: share. Named Dove; let it run
Adds Hawk; spells out hawk-vs-dove (half food, 50% odds) and hawk-vs-hawk (zero food) rules
Pause and predict, then run: mixture hovers near half, fewer creatures total
Not for the good of the species; start all-hawk, add one dove, same mixture appears
Survival of the fittest fails here: no single fittest strategy
Rules turned into a payoff table after they were watched in action
I control top blob, you control left; if I play hawk, you should back down
Repeated play with memory would change things; these blobs meet once and forget
Same reasoning for the dove case; arrows drawn; rows filled with less detail
Two stable cells; only then named game theory and Nash equilibrium
Best strategy is the opposite of the opponent; population pulled to an equilibrium fraction
Equilibrium defined as equal expected scores for both strategies
Pause and compute the hawk score yourself; 1.35, so 90% is not equilibrium
Swap numbers for variables; admits it is a lot of letters, then removes one via h=1-d
Graph both score lines; crossing at 50% doves
Big simulation confirms the prediction; admits it feels like a lot of work for a known answer
Change hawk-hawk payoff to 1/4: equilibrium shifts to 1/3 doves, confirmed by simulation
Previews mixed, conditional, and asymmetric strategies with real-animal links
Payoff 3/4: lines never cross, arrows flip, everyone fights
Names it the prisoner's dilemma; promises ways out later

metrics.misconception: yes: survival of the fittest implies one best strategy; also selection does not act for the good of the species
metrics.brute_force: yes 7:55: plug in a guessed 90% doves before using variables
metrics.examples: 4 payoff settings (0, then 0 at large scale, 1/4, 3/4) plus 3 starting populations (all dove, all hawk, hawk added); each new number tests the same machinery
metrics.ending: Teasers that end at a parameter change turning the model into the prisoner's dilemma, then thanks

new_moves.name: dignify-then-dismiss-the-human-intuition
new_moves.what: Raises the clever human move (retaliate, reward kindness) and explains why the toy creature cannot use it
new_moves.evidence: 5:28 and 6:03 repeated-game reasoning ruled out because blobs forget

new_moves.name: parameter-dial-ending
new_moves.what: Turns one payoff number until the model breaks into a named classic problem

new_moves.name: redundancy-acknowledgement
new_moves.what: Admits the math only confirmed the sim, then shows the payoff it unlocks

theory: The simulation gives the answer first and the math earns its place by explaining and then extending it. Each formal layer (table, arrows, variables, graph) is introduced only once the result it encodes has been seen, and its value is proved by changing one parameter and predicting a result the sim then confirms.
velocity: Orchestrator: run the sim before any notation; use the formal layer only to explain what was already seen, then to predict a new run
Scene builder: give payoff grids a dial on one cell, with the sim and the crossing graph updating live
Voice: when the learner reaches for a human strategy, acknowledge it and state which model assumption rules it out
Ghost hands: write the first case in full, then fill symmetric cases quickly with 'same reasoning'
Evals: check that a predict prompt is shown before each sim reveal
quote: the best strategy isn't hawk or dove
